name: Pure Polynucleotide (PDRN)

lead: PDRN (polydeoxyribonucleotide) is a mixture of DNA fragments, today mostly purified from salmon or trout, injected into the skin as a 'skin booster'. People use it for better skin texture, softer scars and fewer fine lines, often as an alternative or add-on to hyaluronic acid boosters.

The idea is that PDRN breaks down into components such as adenosine, which acts on the A2A receptor and is linked in lab work to blood-vessel growth and tissue-repair signalling, so skin quality and healing improve. Human trials so far mostly cover wounds, tendons and joints, with cosmetic scar and wrinkle trials registered but small and recent.

paras: It is a clinic procedure: a clinician places small deposits into the skin of the face or other areas, usually as a short series of sessions, and it is sometimes combined with other skin treatments. Users typically look for gradual changes in texture and healing over the weeks after sessions.

Reported adverse effects in the trials surveyed are generally minor, and purified products are described as having low immunogenicity. Injection-site reactions and the usual risks of intradermal procedures apply. Regulatory status differs by country and product, being a medicine in some places and a device or cosmetic in others.

angle.text: PDRN is an injectable salmon-derived skin booster, borrowed from wound-care medicine, that people use for better skin texture, softer scars and fewer signs of aging. It works by supporting the skin's repair signalling so quality and healing improve. Human trials so far mostly cover wounds and tendons, with cosmetic studies still small.

lead: Polydeoxyribonucleotide (PDRN) is a mixture of single-stranded DNA fragments that was first isolated from human placenta for pharmaceutical use in Italy and is now mainly purified from salmon or trout sperm.[1] It is used in wound-healing and tissue-repair medicine and, particularly in parts of Asia and Europe, as an injected cosmetic 'skin booster' marketed for skin quality, scars and aging signs.[1]

Laboratory research describes PDRN as acting through adenosine A2A receptor signalling, with effects on angiogenesis and inflammation.[1][2] Human trials have studied it mainly for diabetic ulcers, pressure ulcers, tendon problems and osteoarthritis,[3][4][5][6][7] while small cosmetic studies have looked at hair density, pigmentation, acne scars and surgical scars.[8][4][9][10] A 2025 systematic review of polynucleotides in esthetic medicine pooled nine studies and 219 patients.[11]

In looksmaxxing and aesthetic-procedure discussion it appears as a 'salmon DNA' or polynucleotide option alongside hyaluronic acid boosters, used by people who want better skin texture, fewer visible scars and a fresher complexion rather than added volume.
infobox: Purified salmon or trout DNA; originally human placenta[1]

paras: PDRN is a polyanionic, water-soluble mixture of DNA fragments of widely varying size. Its biological activity is said to depend on the source and molecular weight, and highly purified products are described as lowering the chance of immune reactions.[1]
Commercial 'polynucleotide' gels used as skin boosters are related but distinct products with their own concentrations and device or cosmetic classifications.

A 2024 review describes PDRN as a registered DNA-derived product made of fragments of roughly 50 to 1500 kDa extracted mainly from salmon at purity above 95 percent, and says in vivo tests and clinical trials have found it non-toxic; it also examines other extraction sources for cosmetic use.[12] A 2021 review of PDRN in skin wound healing attributes its effects to promoting cell migration, growth and angiogenesis and reducing inflammation, acting through A2A receptor activation and the salvage pathway.[13]

Practitioners offer PDRN-based injections for skin texture, photoaging, scars and mottled pigmentation, and sometimes after lasers or microneedling.[1][4] A laboratory study reported that PDRN reduced melanin-related activity in cultured cells, and noted that some patients receiving PDRN injections reported improvement of photoaging-related mottled pigmentation.[4]
A small study combined platelet-rich plasma with PDRN injections around hair follicles in women with pattern hair loss.[8]

The 2025 systematic review of polynucleotides in esthetic medicine included nine studies of low to moderate quality covering 219 patients, with varying injection areas and techniques. It reported improvements in wrinkles, skin texture and elasticity, mild and transient side effects, and moderate to high satisfaction, and called for higher-quality trials.[11]

PDRN has been used for chronic wounds including diabetic foot ulcers, and for tendinopathy and osteoarthritis.[1][14] A registered phase 4 trial studied a placenta-derived PDRN product for diabetic ulcers.[15]

PDRN is reported to be broken down enzymatically, with adenosine activating the A2A receptor, raising cAMP and influencing pathways involved in angiogenesis such as VEGF, and supplying nucleotides to salvage pathways.[1] In genetically diabetic mice, PDRN treatment was reported to stimulate angiogenesis and wound healing, with A2 purinergic receptor involvement.[2]

Human evidence on appearance outcomes consists of small studies. In a trial of 40 women with female pattern hair loss, one group received one platelet-rich plasma session followed by 12 weekly perifollicular PDRN sessions and another received 12 PDRN sessions alone. Hair count rose 23.2% and thickness 16.8% in the combined group, and 17.9% and 13.5% in the PDRN-only group; the combination gave a greater thickness gain, while the difference in count between groups was not significant.[8]

For pigmentation, a laboratory and clinical report found PDRN lowered melanin content and tyrosinase activity in cultured cells, and six women with facial hyperpigmentation who received three intradermal sessions were rated as showing more than noticeable improvement on a five-point scale.[4]

For scars, a randomised trial of 44 thyroidectomy patients gave two PDRN injections on postoperative days 1 and 2. At three months the modified Vancouver Scar Scale favoured PDRN but did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.059), while vascularity, symptoms, erythema index and scar height were significantly lower, with no PDRN-related side effects.[10] A prospective open-label randomised trial of 17 people with acne scars compared air-injected botulinum toxin, PDRN and both; POSAS scores fell 12.0 points with the combination, 9.0 with botulinum toxin and 6.1 with PDRN alone, and treatments were well tolerated.[9]

Outside cosmetics, a randomised trial of pressure ulcers reported that PDRN (n=11) reduced wound size and PUSH scores more than control (n=12) after four weeks with no adverse effects.[7] Randomised trials include a saline-controlled trial and a corticosteroid comparison in chronic plantar fasciitis,[3][6] a retrospective comparison in supraspinatus tendinopathy,[5] and a meta-analysis for knee osteoarthritis.[14] Animal studies have examined tendon injuries.[16][17][18]

Registered cosmetic trials include PDRN for post-operative scars (completed, n=22),[19] periocular wrinkles,[20] rolling acne scars compared with non-crosslinked hyaluronic acid,[21] and facial scars with fractional CO2 laser.[22] Results from these registrations have not been published.

The wound-healing mouse study described PDRN as having no toxic or adverse effect.[2] Reviews describe highly purified material as minimising immunological side effects,[1] although human cosmetic safety data remain limited to small studies. As with other injections, local reactions can occur.
The thyroidectomy scar trial reported no PDRN-related side effects, and the acne-scar trial reported minor swelling and redness.[10][9]

PDRN has been popular in South Korea's dermatology market, where Wikipedia describes it as a common biostimulator after procedures such as laser or microneedling.[1] The term 'salmon DNA facial' has appeared in social media and press coverage; its community discussion is not documented in detail here.

lore.intro: Discussion of PDRN is mostly in clinic marketing and aesthetic-medicine channels, where it is presented as 'regenerative'. Forum material was not available for this entry.
